Indian rhinoceros :: Ecology and behaviour :: Reproduction :: chunk_0010
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/One_horned_rhino_with_a_baby_in_Kaziranga_National_Park%2C_Assam.jpg/250px-One_horned_rhino_with_a_baby_in_Kaziranga_National_Park%2C_Assam.jpg)](/wiki/File:One_horned_rhino_with_a_baby_in_Kaziranga_National_Park,_Assam.jpg)

Indian rhino cow with calf

Captive bulls breed at five years of age, but wild bulls attain dominance much later when they are larger. In one five-year field study, only one Indian rhino estimated to be younger than 15 years mated successfully. Captive cows breed as young as four years of age, but in the wild, they usually start breeding only when six years old, which likely indicates they need to be large enough to avoid being killed by aggressive bulls.[[18]](#cite_note-dinerstein03-18) In the wild, females reach full maturity at about 6.5 years, and males at about 10 years.[[17]](#cite_note-Laurie1983-17) The [ovarian cycle](/wiki/Ovarian_cycle "Ovarian cycle") lasts 5.5 to 9 weeks on average.[[44]](#cite_note-44) Their [gestation](/wiki/Gestation "Gestation") period is around 15.7 months, and birth interval ranges from 34 to 51 months.[[18]](#cite_note-dinerstein03-18) An estimated 10% of calves will die before maturity. This is mainly attributed to predatory attacks from [tigers](/wiki/Tiger "Tiger") (*Panthera tigris*).[[45]](#cite_note-45) In captivity, four Indian rhinos lived over 40 years, the oldest living to be 47.[[17]](#cite_note-Laurie1983-17)[[22]](#cite_note-Panigrahi,_G._K.-22)

A MITS [Altair 8800](/wiki/Altair_8800 "Altair 8800") Computer with 8-inch (200 mm) floppy disk system, whose first programming language was Microsoft's founding product, [Altair BASIC](/wiki/Altair_BASIC "Altair BASIC")

Gates read the January 1975 issue of *[Popular Electronics](/wiki/Popular_Electronics "Popular Electronics"),* which demonstrated the [Altair 8800](/wiki/Altair_8800 "Altair 8800"), and contacted [Micro Instrumentation and Telemetry Systems](/wiki/Micro_Instrumentation_and_Telemetry_Systems "Micro Instrumentation and Telemetry Systems") (MITS) to inform them that he and others were working on a [BASIC](/wiki/BASIC "BASIC") interpreter for the platform.[[35]](#cite_note-keyevents-36) In reality, Gates and Allen did not have an Altair and had not written code for it; they merely wanted to gauge MITS's interest. MITS president [Ed Roberts](/wiki/Ed_Roberts_(computers) "Ed Roberts (computers)") agreed to meet them for a demonstration, and over the course of a few weeks, they developed an Altair [emulator](/wiki/Emulator "Emulator") that ran on a minicomputer and then the BASIC interpreter.[[36]](#cite_note-thocp1-37)

The demonstration was held at MITS's offices in [Albuquerque, New Mexico](/wiki/Albuquerque,_New_Mexico "Albuquerque, New Mexico"). It was a success and resulted in a deal with MITS to distribute the interpreter as [Altair BASIC](/wiki/Altair_BASIC "Altair BASIC"). MITS hired Allen,[[36]](#cite_note-thocp1-37) and Gates took a leave of absence from Harvard to work with him at MITS in November 1975. Allen named their partnership "Micro-Soft", a combination of "microcomputer" and "software". Their first office was in Albuquerque. Harvard was founded and authorized by the [Massachusetts General Court](/wiki/Massachusetts_General_Court#Massachusetts_Bay_Colony "Massachusetts General Court"), the governing legislature of [colonial](/wiki/Colonial_history_of_the_United_States "Colonial history of the United States")-era [Massachusetts Bay Colony](/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony "Massachusetts Bay Colony").[[13]](#cite_note-13) While never formally affiliated with any [Protestant denomination](/wiki/Protestant_church "Protestant church"), Harvard trained [Congregational](/wiki/Congregationalism_in_the_United_States "Congregationalism in the United States") clergy until its curriculum and student body were gradually secularized in the 18th century. In 1780, the [Constitution of Massachusetts](/wiki/Constitution_of_Massachusetts "Constitution of Massachusetts") referred to it as a [university](/wiki/University "University"), and a new [medical school](/wiki/Medical_school "Medical school") established in 1782 was named the [Medical Institution of Harvard University](/wiki/Harvard_Medical_School "Harvard Medical School"); but this was a new name, not a new foundation. Harvard College soon became the name of the university's undergraduate division.[[14]](#cite_note-Timeline-14)

By the 19th century, Harvard had emerged as the most prominent academic and cultural institution among the [Boston elite](/wiki/Boston_Brahmin "Boston Brahmin").[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16) Following the [American Civil War](/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), under [Harvard president](/wiki/President_of_Harvard_University "President of Harvard University") [Charles William Eliot](/wiki/Charles_William_Eliot "Charles William Eliot")'s long tenure from 1869 to 1909, Harvard developed multiple professional schools, which transformed it into a modern research university. Ohio State was among the first group[[59]](#cite_note-60) of four public universities to raise a $1 billion [endowment](/wiki/Financial_endowment "Financial endowment") when it passed the $1 billion mark in 1999. At the end of 2005, Ohio State's endowment stood at $1.73 billion, ranking it seventh among public universities and 27th among all American universities.[[60]](#cite_note-61) In June 2006, the endowment passed the $2 billion mark.

In recent decades, and in response to continually shrinking state funding, Ohio State has conducted two significant multi-year [fundraising](/wiki/Fundraising "Fundraising") campaigns. The first concluded in 1987 and raised $460 million, a record at the time for a public university. The "Affirm Thy Friendship Campaign" took place between 1995 and 2000. With an initial goal of raising $850 million, the campaign's final tally was $1.23 billion, placing Ohio State among the small group of public universities to have successfully conducted a $1 billion campaign.[[61]](#cite_note-62) At his welcoming ceremony, returning President E. Gordon Gee announced in the fall of 2007 that Ohio State would launch a $2.5 billion fundraising campaign. In 2019, celebrating the university's 150th year, President Michael V. Drake announced the "Time and Change Campaign"[[62]](#cite_note-63) with a goal of raising $4.5 billion from 1 million individual donors.[[63]](#cite_note-64)

Ohio State is the [flagship university](/wiki/Flagship "Flagship") of the [University System of Ohio](/wiki/University_System_of_Ohio "University System of Ohio").[[7]](#cite_note-:2-7)[[8]](#cite_note-:4-8)[[9]](#cite_note-:9-9) Its [political science](/wiki/Political_science "Political science") department is a major department in the field.[[64]](#cite_note-:3-65) It also has notable [applied science](/wiki/Applied_science "Applied science") programs.[[13]](#cite_note-:30-13)

Crocus :: Taxonomy :: Phylogeny :: chunk_0009
The genus *Crocus* belongs to the [monocot](/wiki/Monocotyledon "Monocotyledon") [family](/wiki/Family_(biology) "Family (biology)") [Iridaceae](/wiki/Iridaceae "Iridaceae") (iris family), specifically the large subfamily [Crocoideae](/wiki/Crocoideae "Crocoideae"). Within that subfamily, crocus is placed on the [tribe](/wiki/Tribe_(biology) "Tribe (biology)"), Ixieae (synonym Croceae),[[b]](#cite_note-52) one of five. The Ixieae are then subdivided into subtribes, with the genera *Crocus*, *[Romulea](/wiki/Romulea "Romulea")* and *[Syringodea](/wiki/Syringodea "Syringodea")* forming subtribe Romuleinae. The Romuleinae have been characterised within the Ixieae by progressively reduced aerial stems.[[51]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldblatt_et_al1998312-53) solitary flowers on the stem branches and woody tunics on the corms. They also often have divided style branches. However, *Crocus* corm tunics are fibrous and membranous rather than woody as in *Syringodea.* Also, *Crocus* has a ridged and often keeled abaxial leaf surface, while that of *Syringodea* is rounded, and the midline adaxial translucency of *Crocus* is lacking in *Syringodea*. *[Romulea](/wiki/Romulea "Romulea")* is principally distinguished from the other two genera by generally having aerial stems or at least an ovary at ground level, compared with the other acaulescent genera, other differences include unifacial rather than bifacial leaves and the pollen structure.[[52]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhillipsRix198931-54)[[51]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldblatt_et_al1998312-53)

Within the Romuleinae, *Crocus* is a [sister group](/wiki/Sister_group "Sister group") to *Syringodea*, the two genera forming a sister group to *Romulea*.[[49]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldblatt_et_al2006-50)[[53]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetersen_et_al2008-55)[[15]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarpke_et_al2013-15)

The [2014 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix](/wiki/2014_Abu_Dhabi_Grand_Prix "2014 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix") took place on 23 November[[21]](#cite_note-21) and was the concluding race of the [2014 FIA Formula One World Championship](/wiki/2014_FIA_Formula_One_World_Championship "2014 FIA Formula One World Championship"). Double points were awarded for the race, which was won by [Lewis Hamilton](/wiki/Lewis_Hamilton "Lewis Hamilton"), securing his second Drivers' Championship.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

The [2015 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix](/wiki/2015_Abu_Dhabi_Grand_Prix "2015 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix") was held on 29 November 2015. The race was won by [Nico Rosberg](/wiki/Nico_Rosberg "Nico Rosberg") making it three wins in a row with [Lewis Hamilton](/wiki/Lewis_Hamilton "Lewis Hamilton") and [Kimi Räikkönen](/wiki/Kimi_R%C3%A4ikk%C3%B6nen "Kimi Räikkönen") completing the podium.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

The [2016 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix](/wiki/2016_Abu_Dhabi_Grand_Prix "2016 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix") was held on 27 November 2016. The race was won by [Lewis Hamilton](/wiki/Lewis_Hamilton "Lewis Hamilton") making it four wins in a row with [Nico Rosberg](/wiki/Nico_Rosberg "Nico Rosberg") and [Sebastian Vettel](/wiki/Sebastian_Vettel "Sebastian Vettel") completing the podium and Rosberg securing his one and only Drivers' Championship.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

The [2017 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix](/wiki/2017_Abu_Dhabi_Grand_Prix "2017 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix") was held on 26 November 2017. The race was won by [Valtteri Bottas](/wiki/Valtteri_Bottas "Valtteri Bottas"), with [Lewis Hamilton](/wiki/Lewis_Hamilton "Lewis Hamilton") in second and [Sebastian Vettel](/wiki/Sebastian_Vettel "Sebastian Vettel") completing the podium.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

Main article: [History of Wesleyan University](/wiki/History_of_Wesleyan_University "History of Wesleyan University")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/RussellHouseSmaller.jpg/250px-RussellHouseSmaller.jpg)](/wiki/File:RussellHouseSmaller.jpg)

The [Samuel Wadsworth Russell House](/wiki/Samuel_Wadsworth_Russell_House "Samuel Wadsworth Russell House") (1828), home to the Philosophy department. The building was designated a [National Historic Landmark](/wiki/National_Historic_Landmark "National Historic Landmark") in 2001 and is considered one of the finest examples of domestic [Greek Revival architecture](/wiki/Greek_Revival_architecture "Greek Revival architecture").[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Before Wesleyan was founded, a [military academy](/wiki/Military_academy "Military academy") established by [Alden Partridge](/wiki/Alden_Partridge "Alden Partridge") existed, consisting of the campus's North and South Colleges. As this academy failed, New England [Methodists](/wiki/Methodism "Methodism") bought it and founded in 1831 an [all-male](/wiki/Men%27s_college "Men's college") Methodist college.[[8]](#cite_note-google1-8) [Willbur Fisk](/wiki/Wilbur_Fisk "Wilbur Fisk") was the first president.[[8]](#cite_note-google1-8) Despite its name, Wesleyan was never officially a denominational seminary, though its curriculum and campus religious life were shaped by a heavy Methodist influence.[[9]](#cite_note-:1-9) In 1871, Judd Hall was dedicated; it was named after alumnus [Orange Judd](/wiki/Orange_Judd "Orange Judd") and was one of the earliest academic buildings devoted exclusively to undergraduate science instruction on any American college or university campus.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-nytimes1-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12)

The Wesleyan student body numbered about 300 in 1910[[13]](#cite_note-13) and had grown to 800 in 1960.[[14]](#cite_note-autogenerated1960-14)
